analysis.one_liner: Bans civilian handgun commerce nationwide, allowing sales only by licensed dealers and for licensed target-shooting clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 1997 with no cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to import, make, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport any handgun, with exceptions for the military, police, and (at the Treasury Secretary's discretion) licensed dealers and licensed target-shooting clubs. Handgun owners could hand their guns to police voluntarily and be paid fair market value or at least $25. Violations could bring up to 5 years in prison, and handguns tied to violations could be seized. The bill cited findings that roughly 76 million handguns were already in private hands and that handguns play a disproportionate role in violent crime.
analysis.who_benefits: People most exposed to handgun violence, since the bill aimed to sharply reduce the number of new and circulating handguns. Its own findings argued that a national restriction on handguns for non-law-enforcement purposes would significantly reduce violent crime and handgun deaths [S3]. Target shooters would keep access through licensed clubs, whose guns stay under club control [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime for any person to import, manufacture, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport a handgun, except for the Armed Forces, law enforcement, and as authorized by the Treasury Secretary for licensed dealers and pistol clubs [S2][S3].
Sets penalties of up to 5 years in prison for violations and subjects handguns used in violations to seizure and forfeiture [S3].
Lets owners voluntarily turn in handguns to law enforcement and be reimbursed the greater of fair market value or $25, paid from club license fees and general revenues [S3].

The bill's findings state that handguns play a role disproportionate to their numbers in homicide, aggravated assault, and armed robbery, and that a national restriction would significantly reduce violent crime and handgun deaths [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun owners, who could no longer legally buy, sell, transfer, or transport their handguns; gun dealers, manufacturers, and importers, who would lose the civilian handgun market except for whatever the Treasury Secretary allowed; and taxpayers, who would fund buyback payments beyond what license fees covered [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners and the firearms trade

drawbacks.text: The bill itself notes an estimated 76 million handguns were already in private hands, and it does not confiscate them; owners could keep them but could not legally sell, transfer, or transport them, which raises serious enforcement and compliance questions for a rule affecting tens of millions of people [S3].

It eliminates the legal ability of ordinary people to acquire a handgun for self-defense at home; the bill asserts home-defense value is overstated and other means suffice, but that is a contested judgment many gun owners reject [S3].
It leaves broad discretion to the Treasury Secretary to decide which dealer sales and imports to exempt, creating uncertainty for dealers and shooters about what would actually be permitted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would have been one of the most far-reaching gun restrictions in U.S. history: a near-ban on the civilian handgun market with a paid turn-in option. The potential public-safety benefit is large if the bill's findings about handgun crime are right, but the design had real weaknesses — it did not address the tens of millions of handguns already owned, and it banned transport and transfer for existing owners, affecting vast numbers of people at once. It also never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then its Crime Subcommittee, and no one ever acted on it again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sidney Yates introduced the bill in the House on June 19, 1997 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on June 19, 1997, and to the Subcommittee on Crime on June 23, 1997 [S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — through the end of the 105th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, handgun owners, gun dealers, and manufacturers kept the existing rules unchanged; no one gained a new protection either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Handgun owners and the firearms trade

for.name: Rep. Sidney Yates
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Handgun Control Act of 1997 in the House on June 19, 1997.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Henry Hyde, R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 19, 1997, and its Crime Subcommittee on June 23; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: All other 434 House members
against.what_they_did: Not one member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only evidence is that a lone Democrat sponsored it and no member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill bans the civilian handgun market outright, leaving dealers and makers only whatever sales the Treasury Secretary exempts for licensed clubs or public agencies. The industry's interest in the bill ran against the public-safety restriction the sponsor sought.

Ordinary sales would end, but clubs get a licensed path to keep handguns for members, stored under club control between uses. They would survive in a narrow, licensed form while losing free private ownership of club guns.
